title: Epistola Praefaratoria
author: Nicolaus Judecus

passages.original: qui igitur subjicit angulum trianguli, et latus praedicat, is illud quod alteri accidit, ejus prædicationi subjicit cui accidit, ac ob id prædicationem præposteram et naturae contrariam facit. Quam Aristoteles aut modo prædicationem censet appellandam, aut prædicationem quidem non simpliciter, sed per accidens; ubi igitur prædicatio præter naturam habetur, aut difficite, aut certe impossibile est assertoriam demonstrationem accommodare.
passages.english: So whoever makes the angle of the triangle the subject and predicates the side subjects that which is an accident of another thing to the predication of the thing of which it is an accident, and for that reason makes a predication that is inverted and contrary to nature. Aristotle judges that this should either [not] be called predication [at all], or else predication not simply but accidentally. Therefore, where there is a predication contrary to nature, it is either difficult or certainly impossible to apply a direct (assertoric) demonstration.
passages.notes: "aut modo prædicationem censet appellandam" is probably corrupt. The sense, following Aristotle's distinction, seems to require something like "aut nullo modo" or "aut non" ("either not to be called predication at all"), and I have translated it that way. "difficite" is read as "difficile". "assertoriam demonstrationem" appears to mean direct (ostensive) demonstration, as opposed to the demonstration "leading to an absurdity" mentioned in the following context.
